ASSIST · executive recommendation · evidence-driven development

Should we enter the AI software-development-assistant market?

Not as asked. We probed the one part nobody sells — a verdict on agent-written changes built from executable evidence, independent of the model vendor and measured for error — and this page gives the result and the decision it supports. {{One sentence per branch: A — the prototype cleared its exits; we ask for a six-week measurement pilot with fixed exits. · B — the prototype failed its exits; we recommend waiting, with a review on {{pedro:review_date}}. · C — the sample could not separate the verdict sources; we ask for a budgeted re-run, or we wait.}}

The answer

Do not build another AI coding assistant. Generation is owned and priced by the model vendors ({{E-12}}, {{E-13}}), the independents are priced at acquisition scale ({{E-46}}, {{E-47}}), and reselling generation has "neutral or negative" margins ({{E-17}}). What we tested instead is tooling for evidence-driven development: the team defines what "done" means as executable checks before the work starts, and every change — written by a person or an agent — is accepted on that evidence.

Branch A. The prototype cleared all three exits. The decision requested is a six-week measurement pilot with one or two design partners, with its own exit fixed now.
Branch B. The prototype failed {{which criterion}}. The decision requested is a review date: {{pedro:review_date}}, or earlier if {{reopening condition}}.
Branch C. The 50 USD cap left the comparison underpowered: {{runs:...}}, plausible ranges overlapping. The decision requested is a budgeted re-run of {{assumption:rerun_budget}}, or the recommendation reverts to Branch B.

"Why shouldn't we simply buy their products?"

The CFO's question, answered before the ask. In one line: we do buy them — what we probed is the one thing their position prevents them from selling.

LayerDecisionWhy
Assistants and generationBuy ({{verified seat prices}}/seat)Vendor-subsidised; features copy between vendors in months
Policy, sandbox, budgets across agentsAdopt open source ({{E-32}})Free, backed by a large vendor
Model-opinion code reviewBuy if wantedA model's opinion; cannot run our tests ({{E-50}}) or block ({{E-51}})
The verdict, its measured error rate, the outcome recordThe only buildSold by no one ({{E-50}}, {{E-51}}, {{E-53}}); credible from no model vendor ({{E-34}})

The independence point in the vendor's own words: "agents reliably skew positive when grading their own work", and a second model from the same family "is still an LLM that is inclined to be generous towards LLM-generated outputs" ({{E-34}}, {{E-35}}). A vendor cannot sell a credible verdict on itself, whatever it spends.

What the incumbents have not solved

Writing code got cheap. Knowing whether to trust it did not.

Passing tests is weak evidence

"Roughly half of test-passing" agent changes on a standard benchmark "would not be merged into main by repo maintainers" ({{E-01}}). On whole-repository migrations, 118 runs passed every fixed check; 28 deserved to ({{E-68}}).

Review is absorbing the cost

Across 22,000 developers: "Median time in review is up 441.5%"; PRs merged with no review at all are up 31.3% ({{E-04}}, {{E-05}}). The source sells measurement — said here, as everywhere.

Trust is falling while use rises

Trust in AI output accuracy fell 43% → 33% in a year; distrust rose 31% → 46% ({{E-82}}). Two thirds cite solutions "almost right, but not quite" ({{E-07}}).

Agents can defeat the check

A model trained on coding tasks learned to force tests green — including by patching the test reporter to say "passed" ({{E-75}}). The author of a change cannot be the keeper of its evidence.

The gap: four things nobody sells together

A verdict that runs the customer's own checks

Not a model's reading of the diff. The funded reviewer's checks cannot "run your test suite" ({{E-50}}).

Independence from the vendor whose model wrote the code

The grader is not the author and not the author's family ({{E-34}}, {{E-35}}).

A measured false-pass rate, on the customer's repository

Published by no vendor. Four vendors each claim first place on the same review benchmark.

An outcome record an auditor can read

Vendor logs record actions and cost; none records whether the change was verified or accepted ({{E-53}}).

Said against ourselves: the idea is published, the framing and metrics are published ({{E-40}}), and a competitor valued at 1.5 billion USD is positioned next to the gap ({{E-49}}). The gap is real, and it is narrow — which is why the recommendation is a probe with fixed exits and not an investment.

The product, in the order a change flows

It trades speed to merge, and some good changes wrongly held back, for a verdict the author of a change cannot influence. Full design: docs/DESIGN.md.

From a use case to checks

The engineer writes the use case; the team's own assistant asks clarifying questions — agents guess when tasks are underspecified ({{E-80}}) — checks are drafted; a person approves.

A contract, fixed before the agent runs

Scope, required checks, budget — on a protected branch the author cannot write to.

A verdict of executable evidence, after the agent stops

The customer's tests, a scope check, and the agent's new tests run against the original code, where "they must fail" ({{E-76}}). For LLM applications: an evaluation with hidden cases — pass, fail or inconclusive.

An outcome record for every change

What was asked, what changed, which checks ran, the verdict, the cost. Written once, never edited.

A measured error rate for the verdict itself

How often it passes what should have failed — per repository, re-measured for every model and harness pairing ({{E-36}}, {{E-58}}). This is what no one else measures, and it decides how much human review each class of change gets.

What one day measured

Same tasks, three arms — bare scaffold, prompt-disciplined, and gated — each run {{runs:k}} times in an isolated copy. Three verdict sources scored against hidden acceptance checks neither the agent nor the gate ever saw. The task set is small and ours: an indication, not a benchmark.

H4Whose "pass" can you trust?the product's claim
Question it answers

Is the gate's verdict wrong less often than the agent's own claim and than a model reviewer from another vendor?

How it fits

This is the number that can kill the product. If a model reviewer is already as reliable, there is nothing to build.

How it is measured

All three sources judge the same finished changes; ground truth is the hidden checks. False-pass rate with denominator and plausible range — a rate without its range overclaims on a sample this small.

agent's claim {{runs:fp_claim}} · evaluator agent (other vendor) {{runs:fp_evaluator}} · gate {{runs:fp_gate}} — on {{runs:denominator}} changes, range {{runs:fp_gate_ci}}
H5Can the gate itself be fooled?pass / fail
Question it answers

Does the gate reject every change built to be wrong in a known way — scope breaks, weakened tests, tampered checks?

How it fits

A verifier with one known hole is another opinion. All-of-all or fail.

How it is measured

Planted flaws, written before the gate existed, fed straight to it. Known-good changes fed the same way measure the other error: good work wrongly blocked.

{{runs:flaws_rejected}} of {{runs:n_flaws}} planted flaws rejected · false-fail: {{runs:false_fails}} of {{runs:n_good}} known-good changes wrongly failed
H1–H3Safety, consistency, economicsper arm
Question it answers

Does the gated arm run fewer unsafe actions, pass more consistently, and what does a qualified change cost?

How it fits

pass^k, not pass@1: an agent above 60% on average can fall below 25% when it must succeed eight times running ({{E-79}}).

How it is measured

Unsafe actions counted per arm on trap tasks; pass@1 and pass^k against the hidden checks; cost per production-qualified change ({{E-40}}) with verification cost included — never reported without its quality number.

unsafe: bare {{runs:unsafe_bare}} · prompt {{runs:unsafe_prompt}} · gated {{runs:unsafe_gated}}  |  pass^k: {{runs:passk_bare}} · {{runs:passk_prompt}} · {{runs:passk_gated}}  |  cost/PQC: {{runs:cpq_bare}} · {{runs:cpq_prompt}} · {{runs:cpq_gated}}
H6What the gate addsoverhead
Question it answers

What does the verdict cost in time, money and extra attempts — and does it block good work?

How it fits

A gate that blocks good changes teaches people to bypass it; the false-fail rate matters as much as the false-pass rate.

How it is measured

Elapsed time and dollars added per task; repair attempts triggered; false-fail rate beside false-pass. What the gate saves is the pilot's measure, not the prototype's.

+{{runs:gate_time}} per task · +{{runs:gate_cost}} per task · {{runs:extra_attempts}} extra attempts · false-fail {{runs:false_fail_rate}}

What it costs, said before anyone asks

It adds cost at four stages

Writing the checks (engineers' time — the largest and least known), extra attempts (capped tokens), running the verdict (pipeline time), and upkeep plus re-measurement at every model release. It also adds waiting before merge.

It is meant to remove

Review time that executable evidence could settle, rework and incidents from changes that passed their tests and were wrong, and the risk in the 31.3% of PRs now merging with no review ({{E-05}}).

Whether that nets out is unproven

The prototype measured what the gate adds; only the pilot can measure what it saves. Four numbers decide it — cost per qualified change, reviewer-hours, time to qualified change, and both error rates — reported together, never one without the others.

Where it will not pay

Small low-risk changes; fast new builds where a mistake is cheap to undo ({{E-57}}); teams with few tests, for whom writing the checks is most of the cost.

Working rules behind this page

No invented numbers

Every figure cites a row of EVIDENCE.md verified at its raw source ([P]/[L]), or a file under prototype/runs/. Targets are decisions and are labelled proposed; CFO figures are labelled assumptions, with rates left to finance.

Paired reporting

No throughput or speed number without its quality number; no pass rate without the verdict's own error rates beside it. These are redlines of the design, applied to our own reporting first.

Customer data

The product runs in the customer's environment with the customer's model access. Nothing is sent to us, used for training, or shared across customers; the checks and history that accumulate belong to the customer.

Honest exits

Kill criteria were fixed before the results existed, and a negative result is reported as the recommendation it implies. "Wait, with a review date" is a real outcome, not a euphemism.
